nature-econ-143.title: The production-possibility frontier: what an economy can make
nature-econ-143.text: In one example, 10 more packets of butter cost 5 guns when little butter is made, but 50 guns when butter output is already near its maximum. A production-possibility frontier is a graph showing every combination of two outputs an economy can make when all its resources are used fully and efficiently. It illustrates scarcity, opportunity cost and efficiency at once: more of one good means moving resources away from another. A point on the curve is efficient. A point inside means resources are wasted or idle, and a point beyond is impossible with current resources and technology. The curve usually bows outward because opportunity cost rises, as resources less suited to a good are moved into it. It shifts outward when labor or capital grow or technology improves, which is how an economy grows. It shifts inward if the labor force shrinks, raw materials run out, or a natural, military or ecological disaster destroys productive capacity. Being on the frontier is not everything: market failures such as externalities can lead an efficient economy to produce the wrong mix of goods.

nature-econ-359.title: Arc elasticity: measuring between two points
nature-econ-359.text: An ordinary elasticity gives different answers depending on which of two points is treated as the start. Arc elasticity removes that problem. It measures elasticity between two points on a demand curve. The base is the average of the two prices and of the two quantities, which gives an average elasticity over that arc of the curve. Hugh Dalton introduced it very early on. Point elasticity instead uses calculus to measure elasticity for a tiny price change at a single point, but it needs the demand formula to be known.
